plain_english: Things themselves don't matter. But how you use them does matter. So how do you stay calm and steady while also being careful — not reckless but not careless either? Copy people who play dice games. The game pieces don't matter. The dice don't matter. You can't know how they'll land. But using whatever you roll skillfully and cleverly — that's your job. Life works the same way. Your main job is this: separate things clearly and say: "External things are not in my power. My will is in my power. Where should I look for good and bad? Inside myself, in the things that are truly mine." But don't call anything that doesn't belong to you good or bad, helpful or harmful, or anything like that.
original_excerpt: Things themselves (materials) are indifferent; but the use of them is not indifferent. How then shall a man preserve firmness and tranquillity, and at the same time be careful and neither rash nor negligent? If he imitates those who play at dice. The counters are indifferent; the dice are indifferent. How do I know what the cast will be? But to use carefully and dexterously the cast of the dice, this is my business. Thus then in life also the chief business is this: distinguish and separate things, and say: Externals are not in my power: will is in my power. Where shall I seek the good and the bad? Within, in the things which are my own. But in what does not belong to you call nothing either good or bad, or profit or damage or anything of the kind.
source_reference: Discourses, How Magnanimity is Consistent with Care

plain_english: So should we use external things carelessly? No way. That's bad for your will and goes against nature. You should act carefully because how you use things matters. But you should also act with strength and calm because the things themselves don't matter. Here's why: When something truly doesn't matter, no one can stop you or force you. When someone can stop you or force you, getting that thing isn't up to you — and it's neither good nor bad. But how you use it? That can be good or bad. And that use is up to you. It's hard to combine these two things: being careful like someone who cares about external things, while staying firm like someone who doesn't care about them at all. But it's not impossible. And if it were impossible, happiness would be impossible too.
original_excerpt: What then? Should we use such things carelessly? In no way: for this on the other hand is bad for the faculty of the will, and consequently against nature; but we should act carefully because the use is not indifferent, and we should also act with firmness and freedom from perturbations because the material is indifferent. For where the material is not indifferent, there no man can hinder me or compel me. Where I can be hindered and compelled, the obtaining of those things is not in my power, nor is it good or bad; but the use is either bad or good, and the use is in my power. But it is difficult to mingle and to bring together these two things—the carefulness of him who is affected by the matter (or things about him), and the firmness of him who has no regard for it; but it is not impossible: and if it is, happiness is impossible.
source_reference: Discourses, How Magnanimity is Consistent with Care

plain_english: Think of it like taking a sea voyage. What can you do? You can pick the captain, the crew, when to leave, and wait for good conditions. Then a storm hits. What else can you worry about? You've done your part. The rest is the captain's job. But what if the ship is sinking? Then you do the only thing you can: don't drown full of fear, screaming, or cursing God. Remember that everything born must die. You're not immortal. You're human, part of the bigger picture, like an hour is part of the day. You show up like that hour, then you pass like that hour. So what does it matter how you die — drowning or fever? You have to exit somehow.
original_excerpt: But we should act as we do in the case of a voyage. What can I do? I can choose the master of the ship, the sailors, the day, the opportunity. Then comes a storm. What more have I to care for? for my part is done. The business belongs to another, the master. But the ship is sinking—what then have I to do? I do the only thing that I can, not to be drowned full of fear, nor screaming nor blaming God, but knowing that what has been produced must also perish: for I am not an immortal being, but a man, a part of the whole, as an hour is a part of the day: I must be present like the hour, and past like the hour. What difference then does it make to me how I pass away, whether by being suffocated or by a fever, for I must pass through some such means.
source_reference: Discourses, How Magnanimity is Consistent with Care

plain_english: How can we say some external things are natural and others unnatural? Think of it like this: imagine we were cut off from everyone else. I could say it's natural for a foot to stay clean. But if you see the foot as part of a whole body, then sometimes it needs to step in mud, walk on thorns, or even be amputated to save the rest of the body. Otherwise it's not really doing its job as a foot. We should think about ourselves the same way. What are you? A human being. If you see yourself as separate from other people, then yes, it's natural to want to live a long life, be wealthy, and stay healthy. But if you see yourself as a human being who's part of something bigger, then sometimes you need to get sick for that bigger purpose. Sometimes you need to travel into danger. Sometimes you need to go without. Sometimes you even need to die young. So why are you upset about it?
original_excerpt: How then is it said that some external things are according to nature and others contrary to nature? It is said as it might be said if we were separated from union (or society): for to the foot I shall say that it is according to nature for it to be clean; but if you take it as a foot and as a thing not detached (independent), it will befit it both to step into the mud and tread on thorns, and sometimes to be cut off for the good of the whole body; otherwise it is no longer a foot. We should think in some such way about ourselves also. What are you? A man. If you consider yourself as detached from other men, it is according to nature to live to old age, to be rich, to be healthy. But if you consider yourself as a man and a part of a certain whole, it is for the sake of that whole that at one time you should be sick, at another time take a voyage and run into danger, and at another time be in want, and in some cases die prematurely. Why then are you troubled?
source_reference: Discourses, How Magnanimity is Consistent with Care

plain_english: Don't you understand that a foot isn't a foot anymore once it's cut off from the body? Well, you're not really a person if you separate yourself from other people. What is a person anyway? A part of a community. First, the big community that includes gods and humans. Then the smaller community right around you — a mini version of that universal one. So what does this mean? Someone has to go on trial. Someone else gets sick. Another person sails across the ocean. Someone dies. Someone gets convicted. Yes, that's how it works. In a world this big, with so many people living together, these things have to happen to some people and not others. Your job, since you're here, is to say what you should say and handle these situations properly. Then someone says, 'I'm going to accuse you of wronging me.' Go right ahead. I've done my part. Whether you've done yours — that's for you to figure out. There's a real risk you might not even notice if you haven't.
original_excerpt: Do you not know, that as a foot is no longer a foot if it is detached from the body, so you are no longer a man if you are separated from other men. For what is a man? A part of a state, of that first which consists of gods and of men; then of that which is called next to it, which is a small image of the universal state. What then must I be brought to trial; must another have a fever, another sail on the sea, another die, and another be condemned? Yes, for it is impossible in such a universe of things, among so many living together, that such things should not happen, some to one and others to others. It is your duty then since you are come here, to say what you ought, to arrange these things as it is fit. Then some one says, "I shall charge you with doing me wrong." Much good may it do you: I have done my part; but whether you also have done yours, you must look to that; for there is some danger of this too, that it may escape your notice.
source_reference: Discourses, How Magnanimity is Consistent with Care
